lead: Standard single-mode fiber loses least light at 1550 nm but has its dispersion zero near 1310 nm, so a 1550 nm link gets low loss and about 17 ps/(nm·km) of dispersion together. Two fixes exist. Redesign the fiber so its zero moves to 1550 nm (dispersion-shifted fiber), or keep the line fiber and add a short length of fiber with strong negative dispersion that cancels the total (dispersion-compensating fiber). Only a few syllabi list these fibers; the design rule is short and the numbers are easy.
prereq: You need: D = Dm + Dw and Δτ = |D|LΔλ from chromatic dispersion.

blocks.text: At 1550 nm the material term D<sub>m</sub> is about +21 ps/(nm·km) and fixed by the glass. To cancel it there, the waveguide term must reach about −21 ps/(nm·km), five times its value in standard fiber. A smaller core (radius about 2 to 3 µm) and a larger index difference do this, often with a triangular or segmented core profile. The result is dispersion-shifted fiber (DSF), with its zero-dispersion wavelength λ₀ near 1550 nm, where the loss is also lowest. It suits one high-speed channel per fiber.

DSF has a weakness with wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM). When every channel sits near zero dispersion, all channels travel at almost the same group velocity and stay in step. Four-wave mixing between them is then phase-matched: three channels mix to create light at new frequencies that land on other channels as crosstalk.

Non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber (NZDSF) keeps a small dispersion of about 2 to 6 ps/(nm·km) across the 1530 to 1565 nm band, positive or negative depending on the type. It is small enough that the accumulated spread over a span is a third or less of standard fiber’s, and large enough that channels 0.8 nm apart (100 GHz) drift out of step quickly. With D = 4 ps/(nm·km) two such channels move 4 × 0.8 = 3.2 ps apart per kilometre, so they lose step within a few hundred metres and four-wave mixing stays weak.

The price is a smaller effective area A<sub>eff</sub>, about 55 to 72 µm² against 80 µm² for standard fiber, so the light is more intense and other nonlinear effects are a little stronger. How much accumulated dispersion a receiver tolerates depends on the bit rate: of order 1000 ps/nm at 10 Gbit/s for direct detection, and about 16 times less at 40 Gbit/s, since the tolerance scales as 1/B².

Dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF) leaves the line fiber alone and adds a spool with strong negative dispersion, made with a small core and high Δ: D of about −80 to −100 ps/(nm·km) in common modules. It sits in a module at an amplifier or receiver site. Dispersion accumulates with length, so the span is compensated when

blocks.where: D₁, L₁ are the dispersion (ps/(nm·km)) and length (km) of the line fiber; D₂, L₂ those of the DCF, with D₂ negative.

blocks.text: For 100 km of standard fiber at +17 ps/(nm·km), 1700 ps/nm must be cancelled: 17 to 20 km of DCF at −100 to −85. Two costs follow. Loss: DCF runs near 0.5 dB/km, so a 20 km module adds about 10 dB. Nonlinearity: its effective area is only about 20 µm². And the cancellation is exact at one wavelength only, unless the DCF slope is matched to the line fiber: the ratio S/D must be the same for both fibers. Always check the edge channels, not only the centre.

examples.question: A 100 km span of standard fiber has D = +17 ps/(nm·km) and α = 0.2 dB/km. The DCF has D = −85 ps/(nm·km) and α = 0.5 dB/km. (a) Find the DCF length for zero total dispersion. (b) Find the span loss. (c) Only 15 km of DCF is available; find the residual dispersion and the spread for a 0.1 nm source.
steps: (c) The 15 km spool gives −85 × 15 = −1275 ps/nm; residual 1700 − 1275 = +425 ps/nm.
Spread: 425 ps/nm × 0.1 nm = 42.5 ps, under half the 100 ps bit period at 10 Gbit/s, and well within a 1000 ps/nm tolerance.
examples.answer: 20 km of DCF for full compensation; 30 dB span loss; with 15 km the residual is 425 ps/nm, a 42.5 ps spread for a 0.1 nm source.

examples.question: The 100 km span above has a dispersion slope S = +0.058 ps/(nm²·km). The 20 km DCF that cancels it at 1550 nm has slope −0.10 ps/(nm²·km). Find the residual dispersion at 1530 nm and 1565 nm, and the DCF slope that would cancel both edges.
steps: At wavelength λ, each fiber has D(λ) = D(1550) + S(λ − 1550).
Slope matching needs S<sub>DCF</sub>/D<sub>DCF</sub> = S/D: 0.058/17 = 0.00341 nm⁻¹, so S<sub>DCF</sub> = −85 × 0.00341 = −0.29 ps/(nm²·km).
Check at 1530 nm: 20 × (−85 + 0.29 × 20) = 20 × (−79.2) = −1584 ps/nm, which cancels the line’s +1584 exactly.
examples.answer: Residuals of −76 ps/nm at 1530 nm and +57 ps/nm at 1565 nm; a DCF slope of −0.29 ps/(nm²·km) cancels the whole band.

traps: Comparing D values without their lengths. 20 km at −85 ps/(nm·km) gives −1700 ps/nm, exactly cancelling 100 km at +17; neither “outweighs” the other.
Forgetting the DCF’s own loss (about 0.5 dB/km) and its small effective area.
Mixing up DSF (zero at 1550 nm) and NZDSF (small but non-zero dispersion across the band).
Dropping the sign: D₂ is negative inside D₁L₁ + D₂L₂ = 0.
Assuming perfect compensation for every channel. Without slope matching the band edges keep a residual.

quiz.q: Give the zero-dispersion wavelength of standard single-mode fiber and of a DSF.
quiz.a: About 1310 nm for standard fiber and about 1550 nm for DSF.

quiz.q: How do a small core and a large Δ move the zero to 1550 nm?
quiz.a: They make the waveguide term strongly negative, about −21 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm, so it cancels the material term there.

quiz.q: Why is near-zero dispersion bad for a WDM link?
quiz.a: All channels travel in step, so four-wave mixing is phase-matched and builds crosstalk between them.

quiz.q: A link has 100 km of fiber at +17 ps/(nm·km) followed by 20 km of NZDSF at +4 ps/(nm·km). Find the total dispersion.
An 80 km span has D = +16 ps/(nm·km), α = 0.22 dB/km. The DCF has D = −80 ps/(nm·km), α = 0.5 dB/km. Find the DCF length and the span loss.
A span is compensated exactly at 1550 nm but not at 1530 nm. Why, and what fixes it?
quiz.a: The line fiber and DCF have different dispersion slopes, so D₁L₁ + D₂L₂ = 0 at one wavelength only. A slope-matched DCF with the same S/D as the line fiber fixes it.

quiz.q: A 16-channel WDM link replaces DSF with NZDSF. What improves and what gets worse?
quiz.a: Four-wave mixing drops sharply because the channels walk off in phase. A small accumulated dispersion now has to be managed, and the smaller effective area than standard fiber keeps some nonlinearity.

beyond: DSF is specified as ITU-T G.653 and NZDSF as G.655 and G.656. In new long-haul systems coherent receivers undo dispersion digitally, and links are often built without any DCF, which also avoids its loss and nonlinearity; DCF and fiber-Bragg-grating compensators survive on direct-detection routes. Search for “G.655 NZDSF”, “dispersion slope compensation” and “fiber Bragg grating dispersion compensator”.

figure.caption: Dispersion builds up along 100 km of standard fiber to 1700 ps/nm, and 20 km of DCF at −85 ps/(nm·km) brings it back to zero; with only 15 km, 425 ps/nm is left. The DCF cancels dispersion, not loss: the span still loses 30 dB.
